name: Dulaglutide

lead: Dulaglutide (Trulicity, Eli Lilly) is a once-weekly GLP-1 injection approved for type 2 diabetes in 2014. Fat-loss followers see it as an older relative of semaglutide that lowers appetite and brings modest weight loss.

It activates GLP-1 receptors, raising insulin release when glucose is high, slowing stomach emptying and reducing appetite, which leads to lower intake and a leaner body. It is labelled to reduce major cardiovascular events based on the REWIND trial, and a head-to-head trial found semaglutide produced larger weight and HbA1c reductions.

paras: It is prescribed as a weekly injection for diabetes. Use for weight loss is off-label, since it is not approved for weight management.
Common effects are nausea and diarrhea. The US label has a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents, and pancreatitis is also warned. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Dulaglutide is a weekly GLP-1 injection that lowers appetite so you eat less and lose modest weight, moving you toward a leaner body. Diabetes trials showed weight loss, and semaglutide produced larger reductions in a head-to-head trial. It is not approved for obesity.

lead: Dulaglutide (brand name Trulicity) is a once-weekly injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist made by Eli Lilly for type 2 diabetes. It consists of GLP-1 linked to a fragment of human IgG4 antibody, extending its duration of action.[1] The FDA approved it in September 2014 and the EU in November 2014.[1]

Beyond glucose control, it is labelled to reduce major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, based on the REWIND trial.[2][3] It also causes modest weight loss, but it is not approved for weight management.[1] The US label carries a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents.[4]

paras: Approved uses are glycemic control in adults and children 10 and older with type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular risk reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease or risk factors.[4]

In phase 3 trials, lower doses reduced HbA1c by about 1 percentage point with average weight loss of a few kilograms; higher 3.0 and 4.5 mg doses, approved in 2020, reduced HbA1c somewhat more with slightly greater weight loss.[1] A head-to-head trial found semaglutide produced larger reductions in HbA1c and weight than dulaglutide.[5]

Common effects are gastrointestinal: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and abdominal pain.[1] Warnings include pancreatitis, hypoglycemia with insulin or sulfonylureas, kidney injury and hypersensitivity.[1][4] The boxed warning notes dose-related thyroid C-cell tumors in rats; relevance to humans is undetermined and the drug is contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2.[4]
It activates GLP-1 receptors, increasing glucose-dependent insulin release, lowering glucagon, slowing gastric emptying and reducing appetite.[1][6]

REWIND, a randomized placebo-controlled trial in type 2 diabetes, tested effects on major adverse cardiovascular events.[2] A meta-analysis of GLP-1 agonist cardiovascular outcome trials examined cardiovascular, mortality and kidney outcomes across the class.[3] Exploratory REWIND analyses examined renal outcomes, AWARD-7 compared it with insulin glargine in chronic kidney disease, AWARD-6 with liraglutide, and SUSTAIN 7 with semaglutide.[5][7][8][9] Trials are registered in pediatric type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease and intracranial atherosclerosis.[10][11]
It was the 63rd most prescribed drug in the US in 2023.[1] No specific looksmaxxing community material was found; it is part of the GLP-1 class discussed for fat loss.
